items.abstract: <jats:p>This essay argues that the unitary executive theory is better grounded in presidential control or direction of executive officers than in plenary removal authority. Drawing on the Vesting Clause's requirement that "the executive power shall be vested in a President," the paper contends that while removal is one effective means of ensuring presidential control, it is not constitutionally mandated. The Necessary and Proper Clause empowers Congress to structure executive offices, including removal procedures, so long as the President retains adequate mechanisms for directing subordinates.<br><br>The essay identifies two alternative methods for controlling principal officers that satisfy constitutional requirements without plenary removal: first, presidential authority to give binding orders backed by removal for failure to follow those orders; second, presidential authority to directly exercise the powers of the principal officer and to void any actions taken without presidential consent.<br><br>The presidential control theory offers significant advantages over the removal view. Textually, it derives more directly from the Vesting Clause, whereas removal authority must be inferred through the residual theory of executive power or the Take Care Clause—both of which face interpretive difficulties. Practically, the control theory avoids rendering unconstitutional major features of existing government, including administrative law judges protected by for-cause removal and the civil service system.&nbsp;</jats:p>
title: The Unitary Executive: Presidential Control, not Removal

title: 7. Board composition—appointment and removal of directors

items.abstract: This chapter discusses the appointment and removal of directors, including corporate directors, and especially considers the recently enacted requirements for identity verification on appointment and addresses the consequences of appointments where the individual’s identity has not been verified. It also considers directors’ remuneration. This chapter addresses the three classes of directors: the de jure director, the de facto director, and the shadow director. The chapter considers the behaviour which will result in being classified as a de facto or a shadow director, explores the extensive case law on these issues, and identifies the duties and liabilities which attach or potentially attach to each category.

This chapter considers three classes of directors: the de jure director, the de facto director, and the shadow director. It identifies the characteristics of each category and the liabilities which attach in the event that someone is classed as being a director. It also considers whether fiduciary duties are owed by shadow directors. The position of corporate directors is also considered. In addition, the remuneration of directors is addressed.
